entries.0e625a1b9f8cf405a2bd670819a8c637134d1db5: <div sID="gen33683" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="1John.3" sID="1John.3"/> <div eID="gen33683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33684" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33685" type="x-p"/> The apostle here magnifies the love of God in our adoption, <reference osisRef="1John.3.1-1John.3.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. He thereupon argues for holiness (<reference osisRef="1John.3.3">ver. 3</reference>), and against sin, <reference osisRef="1John.3.4-1John.3.19">ver. 4-19</reference>. He presses brotherly love, <reference osisRef="1John.3.11-1John.3.18">ver. 11-18</reference>. How to assure our hearts before God, <reference osisRef="1John.3.19-1John.3.22">ver. 19-22</reference>. The precept of faith, <reference osisRef="1John.3.23">ver. 23</reference>. And the good of obedience, <reference osisRef="1John.3.24">ver. 24</reference>.
entries.e34ae9b839b30c85ece60adc6ae28351a60fc5e7: <div eID="gen33685" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33684" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Adoption. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33686" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God: therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not. <hi type="super">2</hi> Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is. <hi type="super">3</hi> And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure. <div eID="gen33686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33687" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having shown the dignity of Christ's faithful followers, that they are born of him and thereby nearly allied to God, now here, <div eID="gen33687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33688" type="x-p"/> I. Breaks forth into the admiration of that grace that is the spring of such a wonderful vouchsafement: <hi type="italic">Behold</hi> (see you, observe) <hi type="italic">what manner of love,</hi> or how great love, <hi type="italic">the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called,</hi> effectually called (he who calls things that are not makes them to be what they were not) <hi type="italic">the sons of God!</hi> The Father adopts all the children of the Son. The Son indeed calls them, and makes them his brethren; and thereby he confers upon them the power and dignity of the sons of God. It is wonderful condescending love of the eternal Father, that such as we should be made and called his sons—we who by nature are heirs of sin, and guilt, and the curse of God—we who by practice are children of corruption, disobedience, and ingratitude! Strange, that the holy God is not ashamed to be called our Father, and to call us his sons! Thence the apostle, <div eID="gen33688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33689" type="x-p"/> II. Infers the honour of believers above the cognizance of the world. Unbelievers know little of them. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> (or wherefore, upon this score) <hi type="italic">the world knoweth us not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Little does the world perceive the advancement and happiness of the genuine followers of Christ. They are here exposed to the common calamities of earth and time; all things fall alike to them as to others, or rather they are subject to the greater sorrow, for they have often reason to say, <hi type="italic">If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.19">1 Cor. xv. 19</reference>. The unchristian world, therefore, that walks by sight, knows not their dignity, their privileges, the enjoyments they have in hand, nor what they are entitled to. Little does the world think that these poor, humble, contemned ones are the favourites of heaven, and will be inhabitants there ere long. And they may bear their case the better since their Lord was here unknown as well as they: <hi type="italic">Because it knew him not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Little did the world think how great a person was once sojourning here, that the Maker of it was once an inhabitant of it. Little did the Jewish world think that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, was one of their blood, and dwelt in their land; he came to his own, and his own received him not. He came to his own, and his own crucified him; but surely, <hi type="italic">had they known him, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. Let the followers of Christ be content with hard fare here, since they are in a land of strangers, among those who little know them, and their Lord was so treated before them. Then the apostle, <div eID="gen33689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33690" type="x-p"/> III. Exalts these persevering disciples in the prospect of the certain revelation of their state and dignity. Here, 1. Their present honourable relation is asserted: <hi type="italic">Beloved</hi> (you may well be our beloved, for you are beloved of God), <hi type="italic">now are we the sons of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.2">v. 2</reference>. We have the nature of sons by regeneration: we have the title, and spirit, and right to the inheritance of sons by adoption. <hi type="italic">This honour have all the saints.</hi> 2. The discovery of the bliss belonging and suitable to this relation is denied: <hi type="italic">And it doth not yet appear what we shall be,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.2">v. 2</reference>. The glory pertaining to the sonship and adoption is adjourned and reserved for another world. The discovery of it here would put a stop to the current of affairs that must now proceed. The sons of God must walk by faith, and live by hope. 3. The time of the revelation of the sons of God in their proper state and glory is determined; and that is when their elder brother comes to call and collect them all together: <hi type="italic">But we know that when he shall appear we shall be like him.</hi> The particle, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ean,</hi></hi> usually translated <hi type="italic">if,</hi> is here well rendered <hi type="italic">when;</hi> for the Hebrew particle <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">am</hi></hi> (to which this is thought to correspond) is observed so to signify, as Dr. Whitby has here noted; and not only is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ean</hi></hi> sometimes used for <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hotan,</hi></hi> but some copies even here read <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hotan,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">when.</hi> And accordingly it seems proper so to render it in <reference osisRef="John.14.3">John xiv. 3</reference>, where we read it, <hi type="italic">And if I go, and prepare a place;</hi> but more naturally and properly, <hi type="italic">When I shall have gone, and shall have prepared the place, I will come again, and receive you unto myself,</hi> or <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">paralepsomai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I will take you along with myself, that where I am there you may be also.</hi> When the head of the church, the only-begotten of the Father, shall appear, his members, the adopted of God, shall appear and be manifested together with him. They may then well wait in faith, hope, and earnest desire, for the revelation of the Lord Jesus; as even the creation itself waiteth for their perfection, <hi type="italic">and the public manifestation of the sons of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.19">Rom. viii. 19</reference>. The sons of God will be known and be made manifest by their likeness to their head: <hi type="italic">They shall be like him</hi>—like him in honour, and power, and glory. Their vile bodies shall be made like his glorious body; they shall be filled with life, light, and bliss from him. <hi type="italic">When he, who is their life, shall appear, they also shall appear with him in glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col. iii. 4</reference>. Then, 4. Their likeness to him is argued from the sight they shall have of him: <hi type="italic">We shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.</hi> Their likeness will be the cause of that sight which they shall have of him. Indeed, all shall see him, but not as they do; not as <hi type="italic">he is,</hi> namely, to those in heaven. The wicked shall see him in his frowns, in the terror of his majesty, and the splendour of his avenging perfections; but these shall see him in the smiles and beauty of his face, in the correspondence and amiableness of his glory, in the harmony and agreeableness of his beatific perfections. Their likeness shall enable them to see him as the blessed do in heaven. Or the sight of him shall be the cause of their likeness; it shall be a transformative sight: they shall be transformed into the same image by the beatific view that they shall have of him. Then the apostle, <div eID="gen33690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33691" type="x-p"/> IV. Urges the engagement of these sons of God to the prosecution of holiness: <hi type="italic">And every man that hath this hope in him purifies himself even as he is pure,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.3">v. 3</reference>. The sons of God know that their Lord is holy and pure; he is of purer heart and eyes than to admit any pollution or impurity to dwell with him. Those then who hope to live with him must study the utmost purity from the world, and flesh, and sin; they must grow in grace and holiness. Not only does their Lord command them to do so, but their new nature inclines them so to do; yea, their hope of heaven will dictate and constrain them so to do. They know that their high priest is holy, harmless, and undefiled. They know that their God and Father is the high and holy one, that all the society is pure and holy, that their inheritance is an inheritance of saints in light. It is a contradiction to such hope to indulge sin and impurity. And therefore, as we are sanctified by faith, we must be sanctified by hope. That we may be saved by hope we must be purified by hope. It is the hope of hypocrites, and not of the sons of God, that makes an allowance for the gratification of impure desires and lusts.
entries.04a68a23df3a55922ac31e620846e5ef5a31ff96: <div eID="gen33691" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Mark of God's Children. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33692" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law. <hi type="super">5</hi> And ye know that he was manifested to take away our sins; and in him is no sin. <hi type="super">6</hi> Whosoever abideth in him sinneth not: whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, neither known him. <hi type="super">7</hi> Little children, let no man deceive you: he that doeth righteousness is righteous, even as he is righteous. <hi type="super">8</hi> He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sinneth from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil. <hi type="super">9</hi> Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. <hi type="super">10</hi> In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God, neither he that loveth not his brother. <div eID="gen33692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33693" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having alleged the believer's obligation to purity from his hope of heaven, and of communion with Christ in glory at the day of his appearance, now proceeds to fill his own mouth and the believer's mind with multiplied arguments against sin, and all communion with the impure unfruitful works of darkness. And so he reasons and argues, <div eID="gen33693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33694" type="x-p"/> I. From the nature of sin and the intrinsic evil of it. It is a contrariety to the divine law: <hi type="italic">Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also (or even) the law</hi> (or, whosoever committeth sin even committeth enormity, or aberration from law, or from the law); <hi type="italic">for sin is the transgression of the law,</hi> or is lawlessness, <reference osisRef="1John.3.4">v. 4</reference>. Sin is the destitution or privation of correspondence and agreement with the divine law, that law which is the transcript of the divine nature and purity, which contains his will for the government of the world, which is suitable to the rational nature, and enacted for the good of the world, which shows man the way of felicity and peace, and conducts him to the author of his nature and of the law. The current commission of sin now is the rejection of the divine law, and this is the rejection of the divine authority, and consequently of God himself. <div eID="gen33694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33695" type="x-p"/> II. From the design and errand of the Lord Jesus in and to this world, which was to remove sin: <hi type="italic">And you know that he was manifested to take away our sins, and in him is no sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.5">v. 5</reference>. The Son of God appeared, and was known, in our nature; and he came to vindicate and exalt the divine law, and that by obedience to the precept, and by subjection and suffering under the penal sanction, under the curse of it. <hi type="italic">He came therefore to take away our sins,</hi> to take away the guilt of them by the sacrifice of himself, to take away the commission of them by implanting a new nature in us (for we are sanctifies by virtue of his death), and to dissuade and save from it by his own example, <hi type="italic">and</hi> (or <hi type="italic">for) in him was no sin;</hi> or, he takes sin away, that he may conform us to himself, <hi type="italic">and in him is no sin.</hi> Those that expect communion with Christ above should study communion with him here in the utmost purity. And the Christian world should know and consider the great end of the Son of God's coming hither: it was to take away our sin: <hi type="italic">And you know</hi> (and this knowledge should be deep and effectual) <hi type="italic">that he was manifested to take away our sins.</hi> <div eID="gen33695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33696" type="x-p"/> III. From the opposition between sin and a real union with or adhesion to the Lord Christ: <hi type="italic">Whosoever abideth in him sinneth not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.6">v. 6</reference>. To sin here is the same as to commit sin (<reference osisRef="1John.3.8-1John.3.9">v. 8, 9</reference>), and to commit sin is to practise sin. He that abideth in Christ continues not in the practice of sin. As vital union with the Lord Jesus broke the power of sin in the heart and nature, so continuance therein prevents the regency and prevalence thereof in the life and conduct. Or the negative expression here is put for the positive: <hi type="italic">He sinneth not,</hi> that is, he is obedient, <hi type="italic">he keeps the commandments</hi> (in sincerity, and in the ordinary course of life) <hi type="italic">and does those things that are pleasing in his sight,</hi> as is said <reference osisRef="1John.3.22">v. 22</reference>. Those that abide in Christ abide in their covenant with him, and consequently watch against the sin that is contrary thereto. They abide in the potent light and knowledge of him; and therefore it may be concluded <hi type="italic">that he that sinneth</hi> (abideth in the predominant practice of sin) <hi type="italic">hath not seen him</hi> (hath not his mind impressed with a sound evangelical discerning of him), <hi type="italic">neither known him,</hi> hath no experimental acquaintance with him. Practical renunciation of sin is the great evidence of spiritual union with, continuance in, and saving knowledge of, the Lord Christ. <div eID="gen33696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33697" type="x-p"/> IV. From the connection between the practice of righteousness and a state of righteousness, intimating withal that the practice of sin and a justified state are inconsistent; and this is introduced with a supposition that a surmise to the contrary is a gross deceit: "<hi type="italic">Little children,</hi> dear children, and as much children as you are, herein <hi type="italic">let no man deceive you.</hi> There will be those who will magnify your new light and entertainment of Christianity, who will make you believe that your knowledge, profession, and baptism, will excuse you from the care and accuracy of the Christian life. But beware of such self-deceit. <hi type="italic">He that doeth righteousness in righteous.</hi>" It may appear that righteousness may in several places of scripture be justly rendered <hi type="italic">religion,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Matt.5.10">Matt. v. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Blessed are those that are persecuted for righteousness' sake,</hi> that is, for religion's sake; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.14">1 Pet. iii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">But if you suffer for righteousness' sake</hi> (religion's sake) <hi type="italic">happy are you;</hi> and <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">2 Tim. iii. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">All scripture,</hi> or the whole scripture, <hi type="italic">is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine—and for instruction in righteousness,</hi> that is, in the nature and branches of religion. To do righteousness then, especially being set in opposition to the doing, committing, or practising, of sin, is to practise religion. Now he who practiseth religion is righteous; he is the righteous person on all accounts; he is sincere and upright before God. The practice of religion cannot subsist without a principle of integrity and conscience. He has that righteousness which consists in pardon of sin and right to life, founded upon the imputation of the Mediator's righteousness. He has a title <hi type="italic">to the crown of righteousness, which the righteous Judge will give,</hi> according to his covenant and promise, <hi type="italic">to those that love his appearing,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2 Tim. iv. 8</reference>. He has communion with Christ, in conformity to the divine law, being in some measure practically righteous as he; and he has communion with him in the justified state, being now relatively righteous together with him. <div eID="gen33697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33698" type="x-p"/> V. From the relation between the sinner and the devil, and thereupon from the design and office of the Lord Christ against the devil. 1. From the relation between the sinner and the devil. As elsewhere sinners and saints are distinguished (though even saints are sinners largely so called), <hi type="italic">so to commit sin</hi> is here so to practise it as sinners do, that are distinguished from saints, to live under the power and dominion of it; and he who does so <hi type="italic">is of the devil;</hi> his sinful nature is inspired by, and agreeable and pleasing to, the devil; and he belongs to the party, and interest, and kingdom of the devil. It is he that is the author and patron of sin, and has been a practitioner of it, a tempter and instigator to it, even from the beginning of the world. And thereupon we must see how he argues. 2. From the design and office of the Lord Christ against the devil: <hi type="italic">For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.8">v. 8</reference>. The devil has designed and endeavoured to ruin the work of God in this world. The Son of God has undertaken the holy war against him. He came into our world, and was manifested in our flesh, that he might conquer him and dissolve his works. Sin will he loosen and dissolve more and more, till he has quite destroyed it. Let not us serve or indulge what the Son of God came to destroy. <div eID="gen33698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33699" type="x-p"/> VI. From the connection between regeneration and the relinquishment of sin: <hi type="italic">Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin.</hi> To be born of God is to be inwardly renewed, and restored to a holy integrity or rectitude of nature by the power of the Spirit of God. <hi type="italic">Such a one committeth not sin,</hi> does not work iniquity nor practise disobedience, which is contrary to his new nature and the regenerate complexion of his spirit; for, as the apostle adds, <hi type="italic">his seed remaineth in him,</hi> either the word of God in its light and power <hi type="italic">remaineth in him</hi> (as <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.23">1 Pet. i. 23</reference>, <hi type="italic">Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever</hi>), or, <hi type="italic">that which is born of the Spirit is spirit;</hi> the spiritual seminal principle of holiness remaineth in him. Renewing grace is an abiding principle. Religion, in the spring of it, is not an art, an acquired dexterity and skill, but a new nature. And thereupon the consequence is the regenerate person <hi type="italic">cannot sin.</hi> That he cannot commit an act of sin, I suppose no judicious interpreter understands. This would be contrary to <reference osisRef="1John.1.9">ch. i. 9</reference>, where it is made our duty to confess our sins, and supposed that our privilege thereupon is to have our sins forgiven. <hi type="italic">He therefore cannot sin,</hi> in the sense in which the apostle says, <hi type="italic">he cannot commit sin.</hi> He cannot continue in the course and practice of sin. He cannot so sin as to denominate him a sinner in opposition to a saint or servant of God. Again, he cannot sin comparatively, as he did before he was born of God, and as others do that are not so. And the reason is <hi type="italic">because he is born of God,</hi> which will amount to all this inhibition and impediment. 1. There is a light in his mind which shows him the evil and malignity of sin. 2. There is that bias upon his heart which disposes him to loathe and hate sin. 3. There is the spiritual seminal principle or disposition, that breaks the force and fulness of the sinful acts. They proceed not from such plenary power of corruption as they do in others, nor obtain that plenitude of heart, spirit, and consent, which they do in others. <hi type="italic">The spirit lusteth against the flesh.</hi> And therefore in respect to such sin it may be said, <hi type="italic">It is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.</hi> It is not reckoned the person's sin, in the gospel account, where the bent and frame of the mind and spirit are against it. Then, 4. There is a disposition for humiliation and repentance for sin, when it has been committed. <hi type="italic">He that is born of God cannot sin.</hi> Here we may call to mind the usual distinction of natural and moral impotency. The unregenerate person is morally unable for what is religiously good. The regenerate person is happily disabled for sin. There is a restraint, an embargo (as we may say), laid upon his sinning powers. It goes against him sedately and deliberately to sin. We usually say of a person of known integrity, "He cannot lie, he cannot cheat, and commit other enormities." <hi type="italic">How can I commit this great wickedness, and sin against God!</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.39.9">Gen. xxxix. 9</reference>. And so those who persist in a sinful life sufficiently demonstrate that they are not born of God. <div eID="gen33699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33700" type="x-p"/> VII. From the discrimination between the children of God and the children of the devil. They have their distinct characters. <hi type="italic">In this the children of God are manifest and the children of the devil,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.10">v. 10</reference>. In the world (according to the old distinction) there are the seed of God and the seed of the serpent. Now the seed of the serpent is known by these two signatures:—1. By neglect of religion: <hi type="italic">Whosoever doeth not righteously</hi> (omits and disregards the rights and dues of God; for religion is but our righteousness towards God, or giving him his due, and whosoever does not conscientiously do this) <hi type="italic">is not of God,</hi> but, on the contrary, of the devil. The devil is the father of unrighteous or irreligious souls. And, 2. By hatred of fellow-christians: <hi type="italic">Neither he that loveth not his brother,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.10">v. 10</reference>. True Christians are to be loved for God's and Christ's sake. Those who so love them not, but despise, and hate, and persecute them, have the serpentine nature still abiding in them.
entries.a9ed85cf7a7d5ca34de16c2cf6228a7817e855d2: <div eID="gen33700" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Brotherly Love. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33701" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another. <hi type="super">12</hi> Not as Cain, <hi type="italic">who</hi> was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous. <hi type="super">13</hi> Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you. <div eID="gen33701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33702" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having intimated that one mark of the devil's children is hatred of the brethren, takes occasion thence, <div eID="gen33702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33703" type="x-p"/> I. To recommend fraternal Christian love, and that from the excellence, or antiquity, or primariness of the injunction relating thereto: <hi type="italic">And this is the message</hi> (the errand or charge) <hi type="italic">which you heard from the beginning</hi> (this came among the principal parts of practical Christianity), <hi type="italic">that we should love one another,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.11">v. 11</reference>. We should love the Lord Jesus, and value his love, and consequently love all the objects of it, and thereupon all our brethren in Christ. <div eID="gen33703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33704" type="x-p"/> II. To dissuade from what is contrary thereto, all ill-will towards the brethren, and that by the example of Cain. His envy and malignity should deter us from harbouring the like passion, and that upon these accounts:—1. It showed that he was as the first-born of the serpent's seed; even he, the eldest son of the first man, was of <hi type="italic">the wicked one.</hi> He imitated and resembled the first wicked one, the devil. 2. His ill-will had no restraint; it proceeded so far as to contrive and accomplish murder, and that of a near relation, and that in the beginning of the world, when there were but few to replenish it. <hi type="italic">He slew his brother,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.12">v. 12</reference>. Sin, indulged, knows no bound. And, 3. It proceeded so far, and had in it so much of the devil, that he murdered his brother for religion's sake. He was vexed with the superiority of Abel's service, and envied him the favour and acceptance he had with God. And for these he martyred his brother. <hi type="italic">And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.12">v. 12</reference>. Ill-will will teach us to hate and revenge what we should admire and imitate. And then, <div eID="gen33704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33705" type="x-p"/> III. To infer that it is no wonder that good men are so served now: <hi type="italic">Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.13">v. 13</reference>. The serpentine nature still continues in the world. The great serpent himself reigns as the God of this world. Wonder not then that the serpentine world hates and hisses at you who belong to that seed of the woman that is to bruise the serpent's head.
entries.a994717122f03afafdc303324a048ec5134f4037: <div eID="gen33705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Brotherly Love. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33706" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not <hi type="italic">his</hi> brother abideth in death. <hi type="super">15</hi> Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him. <hi type="super">16</hi> Hereby perceive we the love <hi type="italic">of God,</hi> because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down <hi type="italic">our</hi> lives for the brethren. <hi type="super">17</hi> But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels <hi type="italic">of compassion</hi> from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? <hi type="super">18</hi> My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth. <hi type="super">19</hi> And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him. <div eID="gen33706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33707" type="x-p"/> The beloved apostle can scarcely touch upon the mention of sacred love, but he must enlarge upon the enforcement of it, as here he does by divers arguments and incentives thereto; as, <div eID="gen33707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33708" type="x-p"/> I. That it is a mark of our evangelical justification, of our transition into a state of life: <hi type="italic">We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.14">v. 14</reference>. We are by nature children of wrath and heirs of death. By the gospel (the gospel-covenant or promise) our state towards another world is altered and changed. We pass from death to life, from the guilt of death to the right of life; and this transition is made upon our believing in the Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life,</hi> and he that believeth not <hi type="italic">hath the wrath of God abiding on him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>. Now this happy change of state we may come to be assured of: <hi type="italic">We know that we have passed from death to life;</hi> we may know it by the evidences of our faith in Christ, of which this love to our brethren is one, which leads us to characterize this love that is such a mark of our justified state. It is not a zeal for a party in the common religion, or an affection for, or an affectation of, those who are of the same denomination and subordinate sentiments with ourselves. But this love, <div eID="gen33708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33709" type="x-p"/> 1. Supposes a general love to mankind: the law of Christian love, in the Christian community, is founded on the catholic law, in the society of mankind, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.</hi> Mankind are to be loved principally on these two accounts:—(1.) As the excellent work of God, made by him, and made in wonderful resemblance of him. The reason that God assigns for the certain punishment of a murderer is a reason against our hatred of any of the brethren of mankind, and consequently a reason for our love to them: <hi type="italic">for in the image of God made he man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen. ix. 6</reference>. (2.) As being, in some measure, beloved in Christ. The whole <hi type="italic">race of mankind—the gens humana,</hi> should be considered as being, in distinction from fallen angels, a redeemed nation; as having a divine Redeemer designed, prepared, and given for them. <hi type="italic">So God loved the world,</hi> even this world, <hi type="italic">that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whosoever believeth on him should not perish, but have everlasting life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.16">John iii. 16</reference>. A world so beloved of God should accordingly be loved by us. And this love will exert itself in earnest desires, and prayers, and attempts, for the conversion and salvation of the yet uncalled blinded world. <hi type="italic">My heart's desire and prayer for Israel are that they may be saved.</hi> And then this love will include all due love to enemies themselves. <div eID="gen33709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33710" type="x-p"/> 2. It includes a peculiar love to the Christian society, to the catholic church, and that for the sake of her head, as being his body, as being redeemed, justified, and sanctified in and by him; and this love particularly acts and operates towards those of the catholic church that we have opportunity of being personally acquainted with or credibly informed of. They are not so much loved for their own sakes as for the sake of God and Christ, who have loved them. And it is God and Christ, or, if you will, the love of God and grace of Christ, that are beloved and valued in them and towards them. And so this is the issue of faith in Christ, and is thereupon a note of our passage from death to life. <div eID="gen33710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33711" type="x-p"/> II. The hatred of our brethren is, on the contrary, a sign of our deadly state, of our continuance under the legal sentence of death: <hi type="italic">He that loveth not his brother</hi> (his brother in Christ) <hi type="italic">abideth in death,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.14">v. 14</reference>. He yet stands under the curse and condemnation of the law. This the apostle argues by a clear syllogism: "You know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him; but he who hates his brother is a murderer; and therefore you cannot but know that he who hates his brother hath not eternal life abiding in him," <reference osisRef="1John.3.15">v. 15</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">he abideth in death,</hi> as it is expressed, <reference osisRef="1John.3.14">v. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer;</hi> for hatred of the person is, so far as it prevails, a hatred of life and welfare, and naturally tends to desire the extinction of it. Cain hated, and then slew, his brother. Hatred will shut up the bowels of compassion from the poor brethren, and will thereby expose them to the sorrows of death. And it has appeared that hatred of the brethren has in all ages dressed them up in ill names, odious characters, and calumnies, and exposed them to persecution and the sword. No wonder, then, that he who has a considerable acquaintance with the heart of man, or is taught by him who fully knows it, who knows the natural tendency and issue of vile and violent passions, and knows withal the fulness of the divine law, declares him who hates his brother to be <hi type="italic">a murderer.</hi> Now he who by the frame and disposition of his heart is a murderer <hi type="italic">cannot have eternal life abiding in him;</hi> for he who is such must needs be carnally-minded, <hi type="italic">and to be carnally-minded is death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.6">Rom. viii. 6</reference>. The apostle, by the expression of <hi type="italic">having eternal life abiding in us,</hi> may seem to mean the possession of an internal principle of endless life, according to that of the Saviour, <hi type="italic">Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst,</hi> shall never be totally destitute thereof; <hi type="italic">but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.14">John iv. 14</reference>. And thereupon some may be apt to surmise that the passing from death to life (<reference osisRef="1John.3.14">v. 14</reference>) does not signify the relative change made in our justification of life, but the real change made in the regeneration to life; and accordingly that the abiding in death mentioned <reference osisRef="1John.3.14">v. 14</reference> is continuance in spiritual death, as it is usually called, or abiding in the corrupt deadly temper of nature. But as these passages more naturally denote the state of the person, whether adjudged to life or death, so the relative transition from death to life may well be proved or disproved by the possession or non-possession of the inward principle of eternal life, since washing from the guilt of sin is inseparably united with washing from the filth and power of sin. <hi type="italic">But you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen33711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33712" type="x-p"/> III. The example of God and Christ should inflame our hearts with this holy love: <hi type="italic">Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.16">v. 16</reference>. The great God has given his Son to the death for us. But since this apostle has declared that the <hi type="italic">Word was God,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">he became flesh for us,</hi> I see not why we may not interpret this of God the Word. Here is the love of God himself, of him who in his own person is God, though not the Father, that he assumed a life, that he might lay it down for us! Here is the condescension, the miracle, the mystery of divine love, that God would redeem the church with his own blood! Surely we should love those whom God hath loved, and so loved; and we shall certainly do so if we have any love for God. <div eID="gen33712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33713" type="x-p"/> IV. The apostle, having proposed this flaming constraining example of love, and motive to it, proceeds to show us what should be the temper and effect of this our Christian love. And, 1. It must be, in the highest degree, so fervent as to make us willing to suffer even to death for the good of the church, for the safety and salvation of the dear brethren: <hi type="italic">And we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.3.16">v. 16</reference>), either in our ministrations and services to them (<hi type="italic">yea, and if I be offered upon the service and sacrifice of your faith, I joy and rejoice with you all</hi>—I shall congratulate your felicity, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Phil. ii. 17</reference>), or in exposing ourselves to hazards, when called thereto, for the safety and preservation of those that are more serviceable to the glory of God and the edification of the church than we can be. <hi type="italic">Who have for my life laid down their own necks; unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.16.4">Rom. xvi. 4</reference>. How mortified should the Christian be to this life! How prepared to part with it! And how well assured of a better! 2. It must be, in the next degree, compassionate, liberal, and communicative to the necessities of the brethren: <hi type="italic">For whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.17">v. 17</reference>. It pleases God that some of the Christian brethren should be poor, for the exercise of the charity and love of those that are rich. And it pleases the same God to give to some of the Christian brethren this world's good, that they may exercise their grace in communicating to the poor saints. And those who have this world's good must love a good God more, and their good brethren more, and be ready to distribute it for their sakes. It appears here that this love to the brethren is founded upon love to God, in that it is here called so by the apostle: <hi type="italic">How dwelleth the love of God in him?</hi> This love to the brethren is love to God in them; and where there is none of this love to them there is no true love to God at all. 3. I was going to intimate the third and lowest degree in the <reference osisRef="1John.3.18">next verse</reference>; but the apostle has prevented me, by intimating that this last charitable communicative love, in persons of ability, is the lowest that can consist with the love of God. But there may be other fruits of this love; and therefore the apostle desires that in all it should be unfeigned and operative, as circumstances will allow: <hi type="italic">My little children</hi> (my dear children in Christ), <hi type="italic">let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.18">v. 18</reference>. Compliments and flatteries become not Christians; but the sincere expressions of sacred affection, and the services or labours of love, do. Then, <div eID="gen33713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33714" type="x-p"/> V. This love will evince our sincerity in religion, and give us hope towards God: <hi type="italic">And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.19">v. 19</reference>. It is a great happiness to be assured of our integrity in religion. Those that are so assured may have holy boldness or confidence towards God; they may appeal to him from the censures and condemnation of the world. The way to arrive at the knowledge of our own truth and uprightness in Christianity, and to secure our inward peace, is to abound in love and in the works of love towards the Christian brethren.
entries.5e3d212ce25cba3ada4016a48fd6457c98e1e478: <div eID="gen33714" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Testimony of Conscience. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33715" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. <hi type="super">21</hi> Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, <hi type="italic">then</hi> have we confidence toward God. 22 And whatsoever we ask, we receive of him, because we keep his commandments, and do those things that are pleasing in his sight. <div eID="gen33715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33716" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having intimated that there may be, even among us, such a privilege as an assurance or sound persuasion of heart towards God, proceeds here, <div eID="gen33716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33717" type="x-p"/> I. To establish the court of conscience, and to assert the authority of it: <hi type="italic">For, if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.20">v. 20</reference>. Our heart here is our self-reflecting judicial power, that noble excellent ability whereby we can take cognizance of ourselves, of our spirits, our dispositions, and actions, and accordingly pass a judgment upon our state towards God; and so it is the same with conscience, or the power of moral self-consciousness. This power can act as witness, judge, and executioner of judgment; it either accuses or excuses, condemns or justifies; it is set and placed in this office by God himself: <hi type="italic">the spirit of man,</hi> thus capacitated and empowered, <hi type="italic">is the candle of the Lord,</hi> a luminary lighted and set up by the Lord, <hi type="italic">searching all the inward parts of the belly,</hi> taking into scrutiny and viewing the <hi type="italic">penetralia—the private recesses</hi> and secret transactions of the inner man, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.27">Prov. xx. 27</reference>. Conscience is God's vicegerent, calls the court in his name, and acts for him. <hi type="italic">The answer of a good conscience towards God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1 Pet. iii. 21</reference>. God is chief Judge of the court: <hi type="italic">If our heart condemn us God is greater than our heart,</hi> superior to our heart and conscience in power and judgment; hence the act and judgment of the court are the act and judgment of God; as, 1. If conscience condemn us, God does so too: <hi type="italic">For, if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.20">v. 20</reference>. God is a greater witness than our conscience, and knoweth more against us than it does: <hi type="italic">he knoweth all things;</hi> he is a greater Judge than conscience; for, as he is supreme, so his judgment shall stand, and shall be fully and finally executed. This seems to be the design of another apostle when he says, <hi type="italic">For I know nothing by myself,</hi> that is, in the case wherein I am censured by some. "I am not conscious of any guile, or allowed unfaithfulness, in my stewardship and ministry. <hi type="italic">Yet I am hereby justified;</hi> it is not by my own conscience that I must ultimately stand or fall; the justification or justifying sentence of my conscience, or self-consciousness, will not determine the controversy between you and me; as you do not appeal to its sentence, so neither will you be determined by its decision; <hi type="italic">but he that judgeth me</hi> (supremely and finally judgeth me), and by whose judgment you and I must be determined, <hi type="italic">is the Lord,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.4">1 Cor. iv. 4</reference>. Or, 2. If conscience acquit us, God does so too: <hi type="italic">Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.3.21">v. 21</reference>), then have we assurance that he accepts us now, and will acquit us in the great day of account. But, possibly, some presumptuous soul may here say, "I am glad of this; my heart does not condemn me, and therefore I may conclude God does not." As, on the contrary, upon the <reference osisRef="1John.3.20">foregoing verse</reference>, some pious trembling soul will be ready to cry out, "God forbid! My heart or conscience condemns me, and must I then infallibly expect the condemnation of God?" But let such know that the errors of the witness are not here reckoned as the acts of the court; ignorance, error, prejudice, partiality, and presumption, may be said to be faults of the officers of the court, or of the attendants of the judge (as the mind, the will, appetite, passion, sensual disposition, or disordered brain), or of the jury, who give a false verdict, not of the judge itself; <hi type="italic">conscience</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">syneidesis,</hi></hi> is properly <hi type="italic">self-consciousness.</hi> Acts of ignorance and error are not acts of self-consciousness, but of some mistaken power; and the court of conscience is here described in its process, according to the original constitution of it by God himself, according to which process what is bound in conscience is bound in heaven; let conscience therefore be heard, be well-informed, and diligently attended to. <div eID="gen33717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33718" type="x-p"/> II. To indicate the privilege of those who have a good conscience towards God. They have interest in heaven and in the court above; their suits are heard there: <hi type="italic">And whatsoever we ask we receive of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.22">v. 22</reference>. It is supposed that the petitioners do not desire, or do not intend to desire, any thing that is contrary to the honour and glory of the court or to their own intended spiritual good, and then they may depend upon receiving the good things they ask for; and this supposition may well be made concerning the petitioners, or they may well be supposed to receive the good things they ask for, considering their qualification and practice: <hi type="italic">Because we keep his commandments, and do those things that are pleasing in his sight,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.22">v. 22</reference>. Obedient souls are prepared for blessings, and they have promise of audience; those who commit things displeasing to God cannot expect that he should please them in hearing and answering their prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Ps. lxvi. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Prov. xxviii. 9</reference>.
entries.5126e506f925da810e255078daa282791ef5b8db: <div eID="gen33718" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Commandments. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33719" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> And this is his commandment, That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he gave us commandment. <hi type="super">24</hi> And he that keepeth his commandments dwelleth in him, and he in him. And hereby we know that he abideth in us, by the Spirit which he hath given us. <div eID="gen33719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33720" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having mentioned keeping the commandments, and pleasing God, as the qualification of effectual petitioners in and with Heaven, here suitably proceeds, <div eID="gen33720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33721" type="x-p"/> I. To represent to us what those commandments primarily and summarily are; they are comprehended in this double one: <hi type="italic">And this is his commandment, That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he gave us commandment,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.23">v. 23</reference>. To believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ is, 1. To discern what he is, according to his name, to have an intellectual view of his person and office, as the Son of God, and the anointed Saviour of the world. <hi type="italic">That every one that seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.40">John vi. 40</reference>. 2. To approve him in judgment and conscience, in conviction and consciousness of our case, as one wisely and wonderfully prepared and adapted for the whole work of eternal salvation. 3. To consent to him, and acquiesce in him, as our Redeemer and recoverer unto God. 4. To trust to him, and rely upon him, for the full and final discharge of his saving office. <hi type="italic">Those that know thy name will put their trust in thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Ps. ix. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>. This faith is a needful requisite to those who would be prevalent petitioners with God, because it is by the Son that we must come to the Father; through his grace and righteousness our persons must be accepted or ingratiated with the Father (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Eph. i. 6</reference>), through his purchase all our desired blessings must come, and through his intercession our prayers must be heard and answered. This is the first part of the commandment that must be observed by acceptable worshippers; the second is that we <hi type="italic">love one another, as he gave us commandment,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.23">v. 23</reference>. The command of Christ should be continually before our eyes. Christian love must possess our soul when we go to God in prayer. To this end we must remember that our Lord obliges us, (1.) To forgive those who offend us (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.14">Matt. vi. 14</reference>), and, (2.) To reconcile ourselves to those whom we have offended, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24">Matt. v. 23, 24</reference>. As good-will to men was proclaimed from heaven, so good-will to men, and particularly to the brethren, must be carried in the hearts of those who go to God and heaven. <div eID="gen33721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33722" type="x-p"/> II. To represent to us the blessedness of obedience to these commands. The obedient enjoy communion with God: <hi type="italic">And he that keepeth his commandments,</hi> and particularly those of faith and love, <hi type="italic">dwelleth in him, and he in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.24">v. 24</reference>. We dwell in God by a happy relation to him, and spiritual union with him, through his Son, and by a holy converse with him; and God dwells in us by his word, and our faith fixed on him, and by the operations of his Spirit. Then there occurs the trial of his divine inhabitation: <hi type="italic">And hereby we know that he abideth in us, by the Spirit which he hath given us</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.3.24">v. 24</reference>), by the sacred disposition and frame of soul that he hath conferred upon us, which being a spirit of faith in God and Christ, and of love to God and man, appears to be of God.  <chapter eID="1John.3"/> <div eID="gen33722" type="x-p"/>

entries.34f2f618ca0a27e44f94cd1ba5a7de8f889ce495: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18932"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen40713" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1John.3.1-1John.3.24">1Jo 3:1-24</reference>. Distinguishing Marks of the Children of God and the Children of the Devil. Brotherly Love the Essence of True Righteousness.<div eID="gen40713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40714" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18932"/><hi type="bold">1. Behold--</hi>calling attention, as to some wonderful exhibition, little as the world sees to admire. This verse is connected with the previous <reference osisRef="1John.2.29">1Jo 2:29</reference>, thus: All our doing of righteousness is a mere sign that God, of His matchless love, has adopted us as children; it does not save us, but is a proof that we are saved of His grace.<div eID="gen40714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what manner of--</hi>of what surpassing excellence, how gracious on His part, how precious to us.<div eID="gen40715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love ... bestowed--</hi>He does not say that God hath given us some gift, but love itself and the fountain of all honors, the heart itself, and that not for our works or efforts, but of His grace [Luther].<div eID="gen40716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>"what manner of love"; resulting in, proved by, our being, &c. The immediate effect aimed at in the bestowal of this love is, "that we should be called children of God."<div eID="gen40717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">should be called--</hi>should have received the privilege of such a glorious title (though seeming so imaginary to the world), along with the glorious reality. With God to call is to make really to be. Who so great as God? What nearer relationship than that of sons? The oldest manuscripts add, "And we ARE SO" really.<div eID="gen40718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>"on this account," because "we are (really) so."<div eID="gen40719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">us--</hi>the children, like the Father.<div eID="gen40720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it knew him not--</hi>namely, the Father. "If they who regard not God, hold thee in any account, feel alarmed about thy state" [Bengel]. Contrast <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1Jo 5:1</reference>. The world's whole course is one great act of non-recognition of God. <div eID="gen40721" type="x-p"/>
entries.065ec00b8e8867351feb6337b9c52c8149d176d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18933"/><div sID="gen40722" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18933"/><hi type="bold">2. Beloved--</hi>by the Father, and therefore by me.<div eID="gen40722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>in contrast to "not yet." We now already are really sons, though not recognized as such by the world, and (as the consequence) we look for the visible manifestation of our sonship, which not yet has taken place.<div eID="gen40723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doth not yet appear--</hi>Greek, "it hath not yet ('at any time,' Greek aorist) been visibly manifested what we shall be"--what further glory we shall attain by virtue of this our sonship. The "what" suggests a something inconceivably glorious.<div eID="gen40724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. Its insertion in English Version gives a wrong antithesis. It is not, "We do not yet know manifestly what ... but we know," &c. Believers have some degree of the manifestation already, though the world has not. The connection is, The manifestation to the world of what we shall be, has not yet taken place; we know (in general; as a matter of well-assured knowledge; so the Greek) that when (literally, "if"; expressing no doubt as to the fact, but only as to the time; also implying the coming preliminary fact, on which the consequence follows, Mal 1:6; <reference osisRef="John.14.3">Joh 14:3</reference>) He (not "it," namely, that which is not yet manifested [Alford]) shall be manifested (<reference osisRef="1John.3.5">1Jo 3:5</reference>; 2:28), we shall be like Him (Christ; all sons have a substantial resemblance to their father, and Christ, whom we shall be like, is "the express image of the Father's person," so that in resembling Christ, we shall resemble the Father). We wait for the manifestation (literally, the "apocalypse"; the same term as is applied to Christ's own manifestation) of the sons of God. After our natural birth, the new birth into the life of grace is needed, which is to be followed by the new birth into the life of glory; the two latter alike are termed "the regeneration" (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>). The resurrection of our bodies is a kind of coming out of the womb of the earth, and being born into another life. Our first temptation was that we should be like God in knowledge, and by that we fell; but being raised by Christ, we become truly like Him, by knowing Him as we are known, and by seeing Him as He is [Pearson, Exposition of the Creed]. As the first immortality which Adam lost was to be able not to die, so the last shall be not to be able to die. As man's first free choice or will was to be able not to sin, so our last shall be not to be able to sin [Augustine, The City of God, 22.30]. The devil fell by aspiring to God's power; man, by aspiring to his knowledge; but aspiring after God's goodness, we shall ever grow in His likeness. The transition from God the Father to "He," "Him," referring to Christ (who alone is ever said in Scripture to be manifested; not the Father, <reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>), implies the entire unity of the Father and the Son.<div eID="gen40725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for, &c.--</hi>Continual beholding generates likeness (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>); as the face of the moon being always turned towards the sun, reflects its light and glory.<div eID="gen40726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">see him--</hi>not in His innermost Godhead, but as manifested in Christ. None but the pure can see the infinitely Pure One. In all these passages the Greek is the same verb opsomai; not denoting the action of seeing, but the state of him to whose eye or mind the object is presented; hence the Greek verb is always in the middle or reflexive voice, to perceive and inwardly appreciate [Tittmann]. Our spiritual bodies will appreciate and recognize spiritual beings hereafter, as our natural bodies now do natural objects. <div eID="gen40727" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae856a6e98132e0442853c5e230a7a82fd15db16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18934"/><div sID="gen40728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18934"/><hi type="bold">3. this hope--</hi>of being hereafter "like Him." Faith and love, as well as hope, occur in <reference osisRef="1John.3.11">1Jo 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.3.23">23</reference>.<div eID="gen40728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>rather, "(resting) upon Him"; grounded on His promises.<div eID="gen40729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purifieth himself--</hi>by Christ's Spirit in him (<reference osisRef="John.15.5">Joh 15:5</reference>, end). "Thou purifiest thyself, not of thyself, but of Him who comes that He may dwell in thee" [Augustine]. One's justification through faith is presupposed.<div eID="gen40730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as he is pure--</hi>unsullied with any uncleanness. The Second Person, by whom both the Law and Gospel were given. <div eID="gen40731" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8bc45ded6d7f6c3cc1244ace8e896ca67fb4b7c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18935"/><div sID="gen40732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18935"/>4. Sin is incompatible with birth from God (<reference osisRef="1John.3.1-1John.3.3">1Jo 3:1-3</reference>). John often sets forth the same truth negatively, which he had before set forth positively. He had shown, birth from God involves self-purification; he now shows where sin, that is, the want of self-purification, is, there is no birth from God.<div eID="gen40732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Whosoever--</hi>Greek, "Every one who."<div eID="gen40733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">committeth sin--</hi>in contrast to <reference osisRef="1John.3.3">1Jo 3:3</reference>, "Every man that hath this hope in Him purifieth himself"; and <reference osisRef="1John.3.7">1Jo 3:7</reference>, "He that doeth righteousness."<div eID="gen40734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">transgresseth ... the law--</hi>Greek, "committeth transgression of law." God's law of purity; and so shows he has no such hope of being hereafter pure as God is pure, and, therefore, that he is not born of God.<div eID="gen40735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>Greek, "and."<div eID="gen40736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin is ... transgression of ... law--</hi>definition of sin in general. The Greek having the article to both, implies that they are convertible terms. The Greek "sin" (hamartia) is literally, "a missing of the mark." God's will being that mark to be ever aimed at. "By the law is the knowledge of sin." The crookedness of a line is shown by being brought into juxtaposition with a straight ruler. <div eID="gen40737" type="x-p"/>
entries.85ace9402859cbe2445a1bd7f4d259eee4550f9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18936"/><div sID="gen40738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18936"/>5. Additional proof of the incompatibility of sin and sonship; the very object of Christ's manifestation in the flesh was to take away (by one act, and entirely, aorist) all sins, as the scapegoat did typically.<div eID="gen40738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>another proof of the same.<div eID="gen40739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in him is no sin--</hi>not "was," but "is," as in <reference osisRef="1John.3.7">1Jo 3:7</reference>, "He is righteous," and <reference osisRef="1John.3.3">1Jo 3:3</reference>, "He is pure." Therefore we are to be so. <div eID="gen40740" type="x-p"/>
entries.1eab65c9ae21ae3022d9c5dac01ce97aa85aa451: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18937"/><div sID="gen40741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18937"/>6. He reasons from Christ's own entire separation from sin, that those in him must also be separate from it.<div eID="gen40741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abideth in him--</hi>as the branch in the vine, by vital union living by His life.<div eID="gen40742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinneth not--</hi>In so far as he abides in Christ, so far is he free from all sin. The ideal of the Christian. The life of sin and the life of God mutually exclude one another, just as darkness and light. In matter of fact, believers do fall into sins (1Jo 1:8-10; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2:1, 2</reference>); but all such sins are alien from the life of God, and need Christ's cleansing blood, without application to which the life of God could not be maintained. He sinneth not so long as he abideth in Christ.<div eID="gen40743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whosoever sinneth hath not seen him--</hi>Greek perfect, "has not seen, and does not see Him." Again the ideal of Christian intuition and knowledge is presented (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Mt 7:23</reference>). All sin as such is at variance with the notion of one regenerated. Not that "whosoever is betrayed into sins has never seen nor known God"; but in so far as sin exists, in that degree the spiritual intuition and knowledge of God do not exist in him.<div eID="gen40744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither--</hi>"not even." To see spiritually is a further step than to know; for by knowing we come to seeing by vivid realization and experimentally. <div eID="gen40745" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9875b367671e88944bde99b3b7d2b420fc7e4a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18938"/><div sID="gen40746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18938"/>7-8. The same truth stated, with the addition that he who sins is, so far as he sins, "of the devil."<div eID="gen40746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let no man deceive you--</hi>as Antinomians try to mislead men.<div eID="gen40747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>Greek, "the righteousness," namely, of Christ or God.<div eID="gen40748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that doeth ... is righteous--</hi>Not his doing makes him righteous, but his being righteous (justified by the righteousness of God in Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3-Rom.10.10">Ro 10:3-10</reference>) makes him to do righteousness: an inversion common in familiar language, logical in reality, though not in form, as in <reference osisRef="Luke.7.47">Lu 7:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.47">Joh 8:47</reference>. Works do not justify, but the justified man works. We infer from his doing righteousness that he is already righteous (that is, has the true and only principle of doing righteousness, namely, faith), and is therefore born of God (<reference osisRef="1John.3.9">1Jo 3:9</reference>); just as we might say, The tree that bears good fruit is a good tree, and has a living root; not that the fruit makes the tree and its root to be good, but it shows that they are so.<div eID="gen40749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>Christ. <div eID="gen40750" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdab1ab6273ee584500f1f66e9e428527ae820e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18940"/><div sID="gen40755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18940"/><hi type="bold">9. Whosoever is born of God--</hi>literally, "Everyone that is begotten of God."<div eID="gen40755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doth not commit sin--</hi>His higher nature, as one born or begotten of God, doth not sin. To be begotten of God and to sin, are states mutually excluding one another. In so far as one sins, he makes it doubtful whether he be born of God.<div eID="gen40756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his seed--</hi>the living word of God, made by the Holy Spirit the seed in us of a new life and the continual mean of sanctification.<div eID="gen40757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remaineth--</hi>abideth in him (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1John.3.6">1Jo 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.38">Joh 5:38</reference>). This does not contradict <reference osisRef="1John.1.8">1Jo 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>; the regenerate show the utter incompatibility of sin with regeneration, by cleansing away every sin into which they may be betrayed by the old nature, at once in the blood of Christ.<div eID="gen40758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot sin, because he is born of God--</hi>"because it is of God that he is born" (so the Greek order, as compared with the order of the same words in the beginning of the verse); not "because he was born of God" (the Greek is perfect tense, which is present in meaning, not aorist); it is not said, Because a man was once for all born of God he never afterwards can sin; but, Because he is born of God, the seed abiding now in Him, he cannot sin; so long as it energetically abides, sin can have no place. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.39.9">Ge 39:9</reference>, Joseph, "How CAN I do this great wickedness and sin against God?" The principle within me is at utter variance with it. The regenerate life is incompatible with sin, and gives the believer a hatred for sin in every shape, and an unceasing desire to resist it. "The child of God in this conflict receives indeed wounds daily, but never throws away his arms or makes peace with his deadly foe" [Luther]. The exceptional sins into which the regenerate are surprised, are owing to the new life principle being for a time suffered to lie dormant, and to the sword of the Spirit not being drawn instantly. Sin is ever active, but no longer reigns. The normal direction of the believer's energies is against sin; the law of God after the inward man is the ruling principle of his true self though the old nature, not yet fully deadened, rebels and sins. Contrast <reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1Jo 5:18</reference> with <reference osisRef="John.8.34">Joh 8:34</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.22">Psa 18:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.2">32:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.113">119:113</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.176">176</reference>. The magnetic needle, the nature of which is always to point to the pole, is easily turned aside, but always reseeks the pole. <div eID="gen40759" type="x-p"/>
entries.48528cca1ffbc40bc4f925fc7da9e810222ef429: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18941"/><div sID="gen40760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18941"/><hi type="bold">10. children of the devil--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1John.3.8">1Jo 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.10">Ac 13:10</reference>). There is no middle class between the children of God and the children of the devil.<div eID="gen40760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doeth not righteousness--</hi>Contrast <reference osisRef="1John.2.29">1Jo 2:29</reference>.<div eID="gen40761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that loveth not his brother--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>); a particular instance of that love which is the sum and fulfilment of all righteousness, and the token (not loud professions, or even seemingly good works) that distinguishes God's children from the devil's. <div eID="gen40762" type="x-p"/>
entries.38d3966d57a85e078214013494697123e3d2fe15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18942"/><div sID="gen40763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18942"/><hi type="bold">11. the message--</hi>"announcement," as of something good; not a mere command, as the law. The Gospel message of Him who loved us, announced by His servants, is, that we love the brethren; not here all mankind, but those who are our brethren in Christ, children of the same family of God, of whom we have been born anew. <div eID="gen40763" type="x-p"/>
entries.91f676a274dcaf8cab35f2e9ad1c5ac33458a440: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18943"/><div sID="gen40764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18943"/><hi type="bold">12. who--</hi>not in the Greek.<div eID="gen40764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of that wicked one--</hi>Translate, "evil one," to accord with "Because his own works were evil." Compare <reference osisRef="1John.3.8">1Jo 3:8</reference>, "of the devil," in contrast to "of God," <reference osisRef="1John.3.10">1Jo 3:10</reference>.<div eID="gen40765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous--</hi>through envy and hatred of his brother's piety, owing to which God accepted Abel's, but rejected Cain's offering. Enmity from the first existed between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent. <div eID="gen40766" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfc0d2c0bbdc5d3878a4189ed43fe759d76469f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18944"/><div sID="gen40767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18944"/><hi type="bold">13. Marvel not--</hi>The marvel would be if the world loved you.<div eID="gen40767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the world--</hi>of whom Cain is the representative (<reference osisRef="1John.3.12">1Jo 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen40768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hate you--</hi>as Cain hated even his own brother, and that to the extent of murdering him. The world feels its bad works tacitly reproved by your good works. <div eID="gen40769" type="x-p"/>
entries.59aa45ef4605934a92f245e5381f5b18a0858b18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18945"/><div sID="gen40770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18945"/><hi type="bold">14. We--</hi>emphatical; hated though we be by the world, we know what the world knows not.<div eID="gen40770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know--</hi>as an assured fact.<div eID="gen40771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passed--</hi>changed our state. <reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col 1:13</reference>, "from the power of darkness ... translated into the kingdom of His dear Son."<div eID="gen40772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from death unto life--</hi>literally, "out of the death (which enthrals the unregenerate) into the life (of the regenerate)." A palpable coincidence of language and thought, the beloved disciple adopting his Lord's words.<div eID="gen40773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because we love the brethren--</hi>the ground, not of our passing over out of death into life, but of our knowing that we have so. Love, on our part, is the evidence of our justification and regeneration, not the cause of them. "Let each go to his own heart; if he find there love to the brethren, let him feel assured that he has passed from death unto life. Let him not mind that his glory is only hidden; when the Lord shall come, then shall he appear in glory. For he has vital energy, but it is still wintertime; the root has vigor, but the branches are as it were dry; within there is marrow which is vigorous, within are leaves, within fruits, but they must wait for summer" [Augustine].<div eID="gen40774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He that loveth not--</hi>Most of the oldest manuscripts omit "his brother," which makes the statement more general.<div eID="gen40775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abideth--</hi>still.<div eID="gen40776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in death--</hi>"in the (spiritual) death" (ending in eternal death) which is the state of all by nature. His want of love evidences that no saving change has passed over him. <div eID="gen40777" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a045ec78d78974aad925cf4c65dfc0df0159286: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18946"/><div sID="gen40778" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18946"/><hi type="bold">15. hateth--</hi>equivalent to "loveth not" (<reference osisRef="1John.3.14">1Jo 3:14</reference>); there is no medium between the two. "Love and hatred, like light and darkness, life and death, necessarily replace, as well as necessarily exclude, one another" [Alford].<div eID="gen40778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is a murderer--</hi>because indulging in that passion, which, if followed out to its natural consequences, would make him one. "Whereas, <reference osisRef="1John.3.16">1Jo 3:16</reference> desires us to lay down our lives for the brethren; duels require one (awful to say!) to risk his own life, rather than not deprive another of life" [Bengel]. God regards the inward disposition as tantamount to the outward act which would flow from it. Whomsoever one hates, one wishes to be dead.<div eID="gen40779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath--</hi>Such a one still "abideth in death." It is not his future state, but his present, which is referred to. He who hates (that is, loveth not) his brother (<reference osisRef="1John.3.14">1Jo 3:14</reference>), cannot in this his present state have eternal life abiding in him. <div eID="gen40780" type="x-p"/>
entries.de6bf5cd48cd6053ae3c6d5ff4f36d0870fa9e34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18947"/><div sID="gen40781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18947"/>16. What true love to the brethren is, illustrated by the love of Christ to us.<div eID="gen40781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hereby--</hi>Greek, "Herein."<div eID="gen40782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the love of God--</hi>The words "of God" are not in the original. Translate, "We arrive at the knowledge of love"; we apprehend what true love is.<div eID="gen40783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>Christ.<div eID="gen40784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and we--</hi>on our part, if absolutely needed for the glory of God, the good of the Church, or the salvation of a brother.<div eID="gen40785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lives--</hi>Christ alone laid down His one life for us all; we ought to lay down our lives severally for the lives of the brethren; if not actually, at least virtually, by giving our time, care, labors, prayers, substance: Non nobis, sed omnibus. Our life ought not to be dearer to us than God's own Son was to Him. The apostles and martyrs acted on this principle. <div eID="gen40786" type="x-p"/>
entries.fecfebaf4bd93cdbc789f870fad5c6a1f5b02673: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18948"/><div sID="gen40787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18948"/><hi type="bold">17. this world's good--</hi>literally, "livelihood" or substance.
